stops.narrative: Inspect the protective imagery and distinguish the palace from its modern museum arrangement.
Compare two royal messages without turning a similarity into a claim of copying.
Look at the handles and painted fountain scene. Separate political rights from participation in everyday work.
Keep probable findspot, royal identity and funerary purpose distinct.
Portable imagery suggests circulation; what evidence would locate this particular journey?
Compare an announced standard with excavated administrative documents; uniform rules did not guarantee identical practice.
Compare skilled bronze making and debated purposes with the evidence encountered so far.

conclusion: Lasting records are selective. A ruler’s announcement, a work scene and a funerary object preserve different voices. Serious comparison keeps audience, material, dates and uncertainty visible.

evidence.prompt: Which reading best respects the evidence?

options.text: A royal declaration tells us what a ruler announced; its effects need additional evidence.
options.feedback: Purpose and reception are different questions. A surviving statement is strong evidence of a message, not proof of universal compliance.

options.text: Similar images prove that every maker followed the same route.
options.feedback: Similarity alone supplies neither a traveler nor an itinerary. Provenance and dated contexts matter.

options.text: Political exclusion means people did no public work.
options.feedback: The Agora study distinguishes formal rights from the broader evidence of work and presence.
